description: We are a aeronautical engineers team creating a precise Lunar Landing Site Navigator, we evaluate terrain slope, and vehicle stability to identify optimal, hazard free touchdown zones for the Artemis crew at the lunar South pole.
summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive mission-planning web application designed to evaluate solar power availability and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) line-of-sight communications across candidate landing sites at the Lunar South Pole. Near the South Pole (-84° to -90° latitude), the Sun and Earth remain very close to the horizon throughout the lunar cycle. Because the Moon lacks an atmosphere (0° refraction), surrounding crater rims and ridges can abruptly block solar illumination or sever Earth communications for days. Our tool integrates official NASA/JPL Horizons topocentric ephemerides with LOLA-derived terrain horizon masks to simulate real-time Sun and Earth trajectories across a 360° panorama and polar map. It provides instant power and link diagnostics, exact sunrise/sunset and Earthrise/Earthset countdowns, side-by-side site or launch-date comparisons, and an automated optimization algorithm that scans a full 720-hour lunar cycle to identify the longest continuous operational window with simultaneous solar power and DTE coverage.
details:
WHAT IT DOES & HOW IT WORKS:

Lunar Landing Site Navigator models the complex illumination and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication geometry of the Lunar South Pole through a decoupled, reproducible data pipeline:

1. Topographic Extraction (LROC QuickMap): We extract 8 radial elevation transects (0° to 315° clockwise, ~50 km sampling radius) for each of our 5 Artemis III candidate landing sites from NASA's LOLA 80S 20M ADJ DEM (20 m/pixel).

2. Curvature Correction & 3D Geodetic Modeling (Spreadsheets): Raw radial heights are converted into topocentric horizon obstruction angles (α) using two complementary, curvature-corrected formulations across our candidate sites—a 2D spherical trigonometry projection (R = 1,737.4 km) and a full 3D selenocentric-to-topocentric (X, Y, Z → ENU) geodetic transformation—benchmarked side-by-side on a control transect to confirm < 0.001° variance.

3. Ephemerides Preprocessing (Python ETL): Our Python pipeline (fetch_horizons.py) queries the NASA/JPL Horizons API in AIRLESS mode (0° atmospheric refraction) to retrieve hourly topocentric azimuth and elevation ephemerides for both the Sun and Earth across a full lunar synodic cycle (720 hours), compiling the validated horizon profiles and ephemerides into data/lunar_data.json.

4. Real-Time Browser Simulation (JavaScript): On the frontend, a custom JavaScript horizon engine interpolates these 360° local terrain elevation masks in real time and evaluates line-of-sight clearance—accounting for the Sun's 0.53° apparent angular diameter and Earth's apparent libration wobble.

All raw LOLA profiles and calculation workbooks are documented in our repository's /Horizon_profile_validation folder: https://github.com/ricardom1618-source/lunar_landing_site_navigator/tree/main/Horizon_profile_validation

BENEFITS & INTENDED IMPACT:

The tool enables mission planners, researchers, and students to visually and quantitatively assess operational duty cycles before committing to a landing zone. By pinpointing exact power blackouts and DTE communication dropouts, it helps optimize surface operations, battery sizing, and relay-satellite requirements for Artemis-era robotic and crewed missions.

SPACE AGENCY DATA:

We integrated two official NASA datasets to model Lunar South Pole illumination and Earth communication line-of-sight:

1. NASA LRO / LOLA Digital Elevation Model (LOLA 80S 20M ADJ DEM) via LROC QuickMap: Used to extract 20 m/pixel radial elevation profiles (TerrainHeight) across 8 cardinal and intercardinal azimuths around Artemis III candidate landing sites (such as Haworth Crater and Mons Mouton), allowing us to compute curvature-corrected horizon obstruction profiles (horizon_profile_deg).

2. NASA / JPL Horizons System: Queried via Python automation to retrieve high-precision topocentric solar and Earth azimuth/elevation ephemerides for each landing site's coordinates and mean elevation (elevation_km), driving real-time shadow and Earth-visibility calculations.

Full topographic profiles and validation spreadsheets are available at: https://github.com/ricardom1618-source/lunar_landing_site_navigator/tree/main/Horizon_profile_validation

TOOLS, LANGUAGES & SOFTWARE USED:

- Data Extraction & Ephemerides: Python 3 (requests library) querying the NASA/JPL Horizons System API to generate data/lunar_data.json.

- Cartographic & Topographic Validation: LROC QuickMap (LOLA 80S 20M ADJ DEM), NASA Moon Trek, and spreadsheet workbooks implementing 2D spherical curvature and 3D ENU geodetic transformations.

- Frontend & Simulation Engine: HTML5, CSS3, Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), and HTML5 Canvas for real-time 360° horizon panorama and South Pole stereographic map rendering.

- Hosting & Version Control: GitHub and GitHub Pages for static cloud deployment.

CREATIVITY & ENGINEERING FACTORS CONSIDERED:

At the Lunar South Pole, flat-plane terrain approximations introduce ~0.82° (~720 m) of horizon error at 50 km distance—enough to miscalculate low-angle solar visibility by over a week—so we modeled all 6 sites (5 Artemis III South Pole candidates plus the Apollo 11 equatorial baseline) using two independent curvature-aware methods (2D spherical projection and 3D ENU geodetic transformation), cross-validated against each other to < 0.001° variance. Beyond static maps, we built a continuous-window optimization scanner ("Find Optimal Windows") that automatically detects the longest uninterrupted period with both solar power and DTE communications—with an automatic SOLAR_ONLY fallback when terrain permanently blocks Earth. We also included a dual-site / time-shifted comparison mode and an interactive Custom Coordinates Evaluator that models spherical horizon dip (R = 1737.4 km) for user-entered LOLA elevations.
